baseline.label: Just ask, in this run (10 fresh contexts)
texts: When you leave a city, you'd hand your "social lease" to a vetted newcomer: your standing Thursday pickup-game spot, your seat at the café regulars' table, the neighbor whose cat you feed. You'd vouch for them in person on your way out. That way, relationships built into existing routines outlive any one resident, and every arrival inherits a web of trust instead of starting from zero.

When someone leaves the city, they "bequeath" their routines to a newcomer: their Tuesday 7am café seat, their barber, their running loop, their bodega guy, each passed on with a personal introduction, so the regulars there already know who's coming. Turnover becomes a chain of vouched-for handoffs, and nobody needs extra time or has to risk approaching a stranger cold.

Make every apartment lease include a "social handover," where the departing tenant introduces the new one to their neighborhood regulars (the neighbor with the spare key, the barista, the Tuesday running group) so that friendships are attached to places instead of to people who leave. With this, frequent moving stops severing connections and becomes a steady stream of pre-vouched introductions that fit into routines people already have.

Attach a "social inheritance" to every lease: when you move out, you personally introduce the incoming tenant to your neighbors, your regular barista, and the group chats you're leaving, so your connections pass on with the apartment instead of disappearing. Newcomers arrive already vouched for rather than as strangers, and it takes almost no extra time because it rides on a move that's already happening.

Attach friendships to the apartment instead of the person. Every lease would include a "social handover," where the outgoing tenant personally introduces the incoming one to their regular barber, their neighbor, and a weekly dinner table, so each newcomer inherits a vetted local circle on day one and the city's relationships outlast any one resident's stay.

Make friendships belong to the apartment rather than the person: when you move out, you hand the next tenant your standing rituals, like "Thursday soup with 4B" or "Sunday run with the couple at the corner café," the way you hand over the keys. The social fabric survives the turnover, newcomers get a ready-made life that needs no free time to build, and every introduction comes vetted by a known lease rather than a stranger.

Attach friendships to apartments instead of people: every lease includes a seat in a small, standing weekly ritual with the same neighbors at the same time and place, such as a Thursday-dinner table or a Sunday laundry hour. When you move out, you hand that seat to the next tenant along with the keys, so newcomers inherit a vetted circle that has already welcomed others, rather than having to build one from scratch among strangers.

Tie friendships to apartments rather than people: every lease includes a permanent seat at a standing weekly dinner with the same five nearby units, so when you move out, the next tenant inherits your seat and the group continues. Because everyone at the table is a verified neighbor, the circle never dissolves through turnover, and it costs only one fixed hour a week, it gets around the safety, churn and time problems all at once.

Make friendships belong to places instead of people: every apartment lease comes with a standing "seat" in a small recurring neighborhood ritual, such as Tuesday 7pm soup at the corner bakery, which the departing tenant personally hands to the newcomer. The circle survives constant turnover, fits into time people already spend eating, and every stranger arrives already vouched for by someone the group trusted.

Make every lease include a "social handover," in which the departing tenant personally introduces the incoming one to three people they know nearby, such as a neighbor, a shopkeeper, or their weekly pickup game. Each move then passes on vouched-for connections instead of erasing them, so the city's constant turnover becomes the way newcomers get woven in.

worlds_core.label: World ideas, core mechanism
texts: A register books a fixed recurring meeting for two paired units, so no one negotiates time; at move-out the leaver vouches the newcomer in, so the counterpart's tie continues instead of lapsing.
Moving breaks routines; 8 days of ~3h with one small cohort builds familiarity while evenings are free; hosted meetings then thin only as fast as members' own meetups replace them.
Pinning a resident's recurring purchases to one staff member at a fixed slot turns daily repeat contact into recognition; recognition lowers the cost and risk of each later exchange.
Paid on-shift residents acknowledge whoever enters a marked ward, pass regulars on at shift change and flag absences, so being noticed costs no one spare time; watch-hours mint an anonymous vouch.
Repeat seating with the same verified co-waiters turns compulsory dwell into shared hours; at parting, hours become a once-only joint record that later seats you beside your partner's partners.
A mutually declared tie gets co-placed housing when either party moves, so hours already invested keep accruing via proximity instead of resetting; batched move-ins co-locate newcomers at once.
A paid district hour tops everyone up at once; between hours, a relay offers each outing only to neighbours whose private lean is high, saying 'someone is there', so near-ready ones go now.
A real small request across a tie either gets answered or not; a miss triggers a crew that removes each side's specific barrier, runs a brief joint task, enforces a still pause, then re-tests.
Taps at a fixed post build dated presence records; long, independent records make regulars verifiable to each other, so approach feels safe; a record that shifts with yours is flagged.
Cold contacts (rushed run-ins, disputes, unrepayable favours) breed guilt and avoidance; stripping them from a new tie leaves only warm contact, so the tie is not worn into avoidance.

worlds_how.label: World ideas, how it works
texts: Housing authority or coop pairs each opted-in unit with two others, favouring a renter-owner mix so one side usually stays. Lease covenant: 45 min every other week at a fixed time in a neutral ground-floor room, booked and reminded 48 h ahead for both. 3-month terms end in renew or blameless release; the register re-pairs. Notice to vacate triggers a three-way handover meeting; a steward vouches if the leaver is gone. Pilot: unit-randomized; track attendance and a 3-item loneliness scale.

Address registration triggers an invite to the next cohort: 6–10 arrivals within a 10-minute walk. Arrival leave frees 8 days of ~3h hosted meals with staged mutual disclosure. Then hosted sessions at days 10,13,17,22,30,40,55; a gap widens only if a weekly one-tap check shows self-made meetups. No program mixers meanwhile. Contact details unlock after shared attendance; a separate custodian holds attendance-only completion records.

Opt-in for both sides. Resident names 3–5 weekly errands (café, pharmacy, grocery pickup, parcel desk). A continuity scheduler matches each to a staff member's recurring shift slot; the app nudges the visit time. Each visit opens with a fixed two-line exchange plus one rotating prompt. Registering a new address triggers re-pinning at nearby outlets for day one. A public subsidy pays employers per continuity hour. Research: does transactional time count toward tie-building?

Wards: lit, glass-walled, sound-damped bays at transit hubs; stepping over the floor line means 'acknowledge me', stepping out ends approaches. Each 2-hour shift has two paid resident witnesses, phones away: they nod at each entrant, learn opt-in first names, walk successors past regulars at changeover, and send an opt-in note after two missed usual visits. Logged shifts issue an unlinkable, revocable credential; a ring tap lights green when greeting. Newcomers get a 3-visit welcome round.

Opt-in. Commuter coaches, laundromats, clinics and sport sidelines reserve 4–6 seat tables at fixed slots; an assigner reseats you with the same people each time. To sit, tap a fixed post: two verified IDs within 2 s, each sees name, district and shared partners only once both commit. Posts log co-present minutes. After 40+ h, a pair taps to mint one co-signed, undeletable record of total hours. Arriving elsewhere, you're seated with holders of a shared partner, ranked by the weaker record.

Housing networks (social, co-op, large landlords) run a carry registry: two tenants name each other (max 2 each, renewed every 6 months, silent opt-out). When one moves, the network offers a unit on the other's stairwell or block, or adjacent units if both move, fees waived. Vacancies are released in quarterly batches so arrivals share a floor and a move-in week. Research: does carry raise tie survival and cut turnover enough to pay for held vacancies?

Blocks of ~40 verified households. Each has a private lean switch (door tag or app) that rises with taps, decays, and is shown to no one. A resident heading to the courtyard table taps 'there till 20:40'. The relay sends one message, never repeated, only to neighbours above their learned lean threshold, and only if two qualify; others never hear of it. Newcomers start at a settled neighbour's lean. Every third Thursday a city-paid 90-minute early release by home postcode resets everyone.

Opt-in at lease. Building system routes real asks (parcel, key, tool) from a newcomer to 2 adjacent households; answer within 24h = tie carries. Two misses: a 2-person crew visits, logs each side's barrier (safety, language, shifts, grievance) and applies its remedy (in-person ID check, interpreter, slot choice, mediation), runs an 8-min task needing all, then 7 min seated, no phones, crew leaves first. Re-test in 7 days; repeat ≤4 times, then re-match. After a household's upheaval, redo.

Posts at busy stops log taps from ID-verified NFC tokens. Someone is resolved to you after 15+ tap days over 45+ days. If they appear only when you do, or their arrival shifts when yours does, they are flagged as aligned. To meet, tap Open and pick a grade: nod, name, walk to platform. Mutually resolved Open pairs are sent to numbered pavement marks; both see the lower grade and their shared stop history. Identity is escrowed, released only on complaint.

Move-in booking opens a 21-day window. A paid steward does the newcomer's setup chores to free time. Four verified residents each host one turn, potluck-equal so no debt forms, in a quiet room off the lobby. Day 21: pairs privately opt in; mutual matches are registered as shielded. Then disputes between them go anonymously via the steward, they never share committees or chores, a passing nod discharges all obligation, and the only prompt to meet is a one-ping 'open' flag.

earlier_hook.label: Just ask, the earlier hook test
texts: Turn the churn itself into the supply of friendship by making every move-out a "warm handoff": as part of ending a lease, the departing resident personally vouches their replacement to three neighbors and passes along their standing slot in an existing low-effort ritual (the Thursday stoop soup, the shared laundry hour). Newcomers then arrive already vouched for, with a seat held for them in something that already happens, so nobody has to approach a stranger or find extra time, and each departure strengthens the block instead of resetting it.

Make trust belong to the address rather than the person: when someone moves out, the lease obliges them to spend one hour walking their successor through the building and block, personally vouching for three neighbors who have already agreed to be met, so every newcomer arrives pre-introduced through a chain of trust that outlasts any one resident's stay. Because the handoff is a duty of leaving rather than an extra social event, it costs busy people almost nothing, removes the stranger-danger problem, and turns constant churn from the cause of loneliness into the mechanism that spreads connection.

Make trust inheritable through the one moment everyone already does: moving. Every move-out checklist (lease, moving company, utilities) would include a ten-minute "successor handoff" where the leaving tenant vouches in writing for three neighbors they'd trust, with one line on each ("Dana fixes bikes and likes company at 6pm"), and the arriving tenant and those neighbors each receive it. The first hello then comes with a warm introduction from a mutual friend who has already left, so strangers meet as vouched-for acquaintances without anyone needing time, courage, or a risky cold approach.

Make belonging attach to the address instead of the person: when you move out, the key handover includes a "warm inheritance" in which you personally vouch your successor to three neighbours or local regulars you already trust, who have agreed in advance to be known. Trust then passes from tenant to tenant like a lease, so every move-in starts with vouched ties instead of zero, and the churn that now erases a city's social fabric becomes the way it gets passed on.

Make friendship heritable by address: when you move out, you hand your successor not just the keys but a vouched introduction to three neighbors you've pre-arranged, who have agreed to give the newcomer a 20-minute doorstep coffee in their first month. High turnover then becomes the engine instead of the problem, because every departure passes trust along through a person who has already vouched, so nobody needs spare time or has to approach a stranger.

Make the churn itself the connective tissue: write a "social handover" into every lease turnover, so the departing tenant introduces their successor to three people they already trust nearby (a neighbour, a shopkeeper, a regular at their café), the same way they hand over the keys. Every newcomer then arrives vouched for by someone who is leaving, so no meeting is with a cold stranger, safety rests on one-hop trust, the cost is a single pre-arranged coffee, and frequent moving becomes the thing that rebuilds the network.

Make friendship heritable: when someone leaves the city, they "bequeath" their seat in their local circle (a standing weekly dinner, run or board-game table) to one newcomer they have personally vetted, who arrives already vouched for by someone the group trusts. Every departure then becomes a warm introduction instead of a loss, so the constant moving that isolates people becomes the supply line that connects them, with no cold approaches to strangers and no new time commitment beyond a ritual that already exists.

Make "social inheritance" a standard part of moving: when you leave a city, you formally hand down your three most-used local ties (your Thursday running group, your barista, the neighbor who waters plants) to a specific incoming newcomer, vouching for them once in person, the way a lease or job handover works. The newcomer arrives already vouched for inside routines that exist anyway, so it needs no extra time and no cold approach to strangers, and the city's friendships persist and renew through everyone's constant turnover instead of being lost with each departure.

Make relationships a property of the address rather than the person: when you move out, the lease handover works like returning your keys, and you must personally introduce your successor to three neighbors or local regulars you'd trust with a spare key, who vouch for them in turn. Ties then survive every move because they're inherited instead of rebuilt, newcomers arrive already vouched for (which solves the safety problem), and nobody needs spare time to start from scratch.

Make social trust inheritable: when someone moves out, they "will" their neighborhood ties by personally vouching their successor (whoever takes their apartment, desk, or dog-walking slot) to three people they trust nearby, so each departure hands over a ready-made, pre-vetted circle instead of erasing one. This turns the churn that causes loneliness into the delivery mechanism for connection, solves the stranger-danger problem because every first meeting comes with a warm vouch, and costs no extra time because it happens during the move itself.
